title: Andreeva Wins 11 Games in a Row to Stun Sabalenka
summary:
Mirra Andreeva was losing. Then everything changed.

The 19-year-old Russian was 4-1 down in the first set against Aryna Sabalenka, the world number two, at the WTA Finals. Then Andreeva found her rhythm — and never gave it back. She won 11 games in a row on her way to a 6-4, 6-0 victory that sent her into the last four.

Andreeva, the French Open champion, mixed loopy high balls that wrong-footed Sabalenka with easy power from the back of the court. She hit 16 winners and made only six unforced errors, carving out sharp angles that left Sabalenka scrambling. The only wobble came when she served for the first set at 15-30 down — she answered with three aces in a row.

Sabalenka, a four-time major singles winner, started strongly and held a double-break lead. But from there she won only 10 more points in the whole match. Her shots grew wilder, and she finished with 23 unforced errors. Tape on her knee did not seem to slow her down.

Andreeva was honest about it afterwards. 'I feel like Aryna did not have the best day,' she told Sky Sports. 'I feel like I cannot really take all the credit today. I'm just happy. I had a goal in front of me to commit no matter what and control the things I can control.'

The result means Andreeva goes through as the group winner. Sabalenka still has a chance: the winner of her final group match on Friday against Elina Svitolina will join Andreeva in the semi-finals.

Svitolina kept her own hopes alive with a comeback win over Karolina Muchova. She took a medical timeout for a right hip injury after losing the first set. But she fought back, helped by Muchova's 39 unforced errors, to stay in the hunt.
why_it_matters: Big comebacks show that a match is never over until the last point, and they remind young players to keep fighting and control what they can control, just as Andreeva did.

background_read: The WTA Finals is a big tennis event where the best players of the season play each other in groups, and the group winners move on to the semi-finals.
In tennis, a match is split into sets, and a player wins a set by winning enough games, so winning games in a row can quickly turn a match around.
Top players use different kinds of shots, like high looping balls and sharp angles, to move their opponent around the court and force mistakes.
Players sometimes take a medical timeout when they are hurt, so they can get treatment and keep playing.
